q: Name the pinned lobe.

fig.alt: A side view of the brain with each lobe of the cerebrum in its own color: the frontal lobe at the front, the parietal lobe on top behind it, the occipital lobe at the back and the temporal lobe along the side below. Labels mark the central sulcus between the frontal and parietal lobes, the gyri just in front of and behind it, the lateral sulcus above the temporal lobe and the parieto-occipital sulcus. The cerebellum and brainstem sit below, uncolored.

q: Name the pinned groove.

fig.alt: A side view of the brain with each lobe of the cerebrum in its own color: the frontal lobe at the front, the parietal lobe on top behind it, the occipital lobe at the back and the temporal lobe along the side below. Labels mark the central sulcus between the frontal and parietal lobes, the gyri just in front of and behind it, the lateral sulcus above the temporal lobe and the parieto-occipital sulcus. The cerebellum and brainstem sit below, uncolored.

q: Name the pinned part of the brainstem.

fig.alt: The right half of the brain seen from the midline cut, with the brainstem colored in three parts: the midbrain at the top, the rounded, bulging pons in the middle, and the medulla at the bottom, where the brainstem narrows to continue as the spinal cord.

q: Name the pinned structure.

fig.alt: The right half of the brain seen from the midline cut. Near the center, the egg-shaped thalamus is shaded green, the hypothalamus below and in front of it is shaded orange, and the pituitary gland hangs from the bottom of the hypothalamus on a short stalk.

q: In the front view, name the pinned groove.

fig.alt: Two drawings of the whole brain. The side view shows the folded surface of the cerebrum, its outer layer, and a dotted outline marking where the band of fibers joining the two halves lies deep inside. The front view shows the right and left halves of the cerebrum separated by a deep groove down the midline, with the brainstem below.

q: Name the pinned structure.

fig.alt: The brain cut down the midline with a head outline. A ring of colored structures around the center makes up the limbic system: the cingulate gyrus arching above the band of fibers joining the hemispheres, the hippocampus curving along the bottom, the almond-shaped amygdala at its front tip, and nuclei of the hypothalamus. The thalamus sits in the middle of the ring.

q: Name the pinned mass of gray matter.

fig.alt: A small drawing shows where a vertical slice through the front of the brain is taken, and the slice itself is shown below. Deep in each hemisphere, beside a central fluid space, sit three colored masses of gray matter: the caudate close to the midline, the putamen further out, and the globus pallidus just inside the putamen. The caudate and putamen are bracketed together as the striatum. The band of fibers joining the two hemispheres crosses above them.

q: Which secondary brain vesicle becomes both the pons and the cerebellum?
Put the steps of early brain development in order.
options: A strip of cells along the embryo's back thickens into the neural plate
The plate's edges rise as neural folds with a neural groove between them
The folds fuse, closing the groove into the neural tube
The front of the tube forms three primary brain vesicles
The forebrain and hindbrain each divide, giving five secondary vesicles

q: Mr. Brandt, 52, overshoots when he reaches for a cup with his left hand, and he walks with a wide, staggering walk. The strength in all four limbs is normal. Where is the damage most likely to be?
options: The left side of the cerebellum
The right side of the cerebellum

q: Mrs. Nwosu, 68, has had a slowly worsening tremor of her right hand at rest, stiff muscles, and great difficulty starting to walk. Loss of which neurons best explains these signs?
options: Dopamine neurons of the substantia nigra
Neurons of the reticular activating system

q: A patient cannot be woken by loud noise or pain after an injury to the core of the upper brainstem on both sides. His cerebral cortex is undamaged. What best explains this?
options: The injury destroyed the basal nuclei, which start all movement
The injury cut the corpus callosum, so the hemispheres cannot communicate
The injury destroyed the hypothalamus, which controls body temperature
The injury destroyed the reticular activating system, which keeps the cortex awake

q: Which does the hypothalamus regulate? Select all that apply.
options: Release of hormones by the pituitary gland
The timing and force of a movement while it is under way
Heart rate, through the autonomic nervous system
The relay of touch signals to the cerebral cortex

q: Over several years, most of the dopamine neurons of the substantia nigra die. Predict the change in each.

variables.name: Ease of starting a planned movement
Inhibition of the thalamus by the globus pallidus
Ability to form new memories of events

q: This is the loop the basal nuclei use to select a movement. Find the wrong step.
options: The cerebral cortex plans a movement and signals the striatum
The striatum signals the globus pallidus
The globus pallidus signals the cerebellum
The loop returns to the cerebral cortex through the thalamus, and the movement starts

q: Fill the gap, going from top to bottom through the center of the brain: cerebrum → ____ → midbrain → pons → medulla oblongata → spinal cord.
After a severe head injury, Mr. Osei's brain swells and is pushed down through the foramen magnum, compressing the lowest part of his brainstem. Which change is most immediately life-threatening?
options: Loss of the sense of smell
Loss of the rhythm of breathing and control of the heart
Loss of the ability to form new memories of events
Loss of coordination on one side of the body

q: Signals from nearly every sense synapse in the thalamus on the way to the cerebral cortex. Which sense is the exception?
A small bleed destroys part of the right internal capsule. Which result is most likely?
options: Clumsy, staggering movement of the right arm and leg
Loss of the sense of smell on the right
Weakness of the left arm and leg
Loss of hearing in both ears
misconception: the thick white matter under the cortex has no clinical significance

q: Why does this course call the caudate, putamen and globus pallidus the basal nuclei rather than the basal ganglia?
options: They are made of white matter, and a ganglion is made of gray matter
They lie in the brainstem, and ganglia lie only in the cerebrum
They contain glial cells only, and a ganglion contains neurons
They are clusters of cell bodies inside the CNS; a ganglion lies outside it
misconception: basal ganglia is the correct anatomical name

q: A rare disease destroys both amygdalae. What change would you most expect?
options: Loss of vision in both eyes
Weaker fear responses to real threats

q: Where is the insula?
options: On the medial surface, above the corpus callosum
At the back of the brainstem, under the occipital lobes
In the center of the brain, just above the pituitary gland
Deep in the lateral sulcus, covered by the other lobes

q: Name the pinned layer.

fig.alt: A cut through the top of the head across the midline groove between the hemispheres. From outside in: bone; the thick, two-layered dura mater, which splits in the midline to enclose a large triangular venous channel; the thin arachnoid mater; a space crossed by fine strands; and the pia mater on the folded cortex. Rounded knobs of arachnoid push up through the dura into the venous channel. Veins from the brain surface cross the layers to reach it.

q: Name the pinned space.

fig.alt: A cut through the top of the head across the midline groove between the hemispheres. From outside in: bone; the thick, two-layered dura mater, which splits in the midline to enclose a large triangular venous channel; the thin arachnoid mater; a space crossed by fine strands; and the pia mater on the folded cortex. Rounded knobs of arachnoid push up through the dura into the venous channel. Veins from the brain surface cross the layers to reach it.

q: Name the pinned structure, the main source of cerebrospinal fluid.

fig.alt: The brain and upper spinal cord cut down the midline, with the fluid spaces shaded blue. A C-shaped chamber in the hemisphere connects through a small opening to a narrow midline chamber, then a thin canal through the midbrain leads to a chamber between the brainstem and the cerebellum. Tufts of tissue lie in the chambers. Arrows show fluid leaving the lower chamber through openings, flowing around the brain and down around the spinal cord, and entering a large venous channel at the top of the head through knobs of the arachnoid. The spinal cord has a thin central canal.

q: Name the pinned channel through the midbrain.

fig.alt: The brain and upper spinal cord cut down the midline, with the fluid spaces shaded blue. Arrows show fluid leaving the lower chamber through openings, flowing around the brain and down around the spinal cord, and entering a large venous channel at the top of the head through knobs of the arachnoid. q: Name the pinned chamber between the brainstem and the cerebellum.

fig.alt: The brain and upper spinal cord cut down the midline, with the fluid spaces shaded blue. A C-shaped chamber in the hemisphere connects through a small opening to a narrow midline chamber, then a thin canal through the midbrain leads to a chamber between the brainstem and the cerebellum. Tufts of tissue lie in the chambers. Arrows show fluid leaving the lower chamber through openings, flowing around the brain and down around the spinal cord, and entering a large venous channel at the top of the head through knobs of the arachnoid. q: Put the places cerebrospinal fluid passes through in order, from where most of it is made to where it returns to the blood.
options: Choroid plexus of a lateral ventricle

q: Fill the gap in the path of CSF: lateral ventricle → interventricular foramen → third ventricle → ____ → fourth ventricle.
This description of CSF flow contains one wrong step. Find it.
options: The choroid plexus secretes CSF into the lateral ventricles
CSF flows through the interventricular foramina into the third ventricle
CSF flows from the fourth ventricle back up into the lateral ventricles
CSF leaves through the median and lateral apertures into the subarachnoid space

q: A small tumor pinches the cerebral aqueduct shut. Predict the change in each over the following days.

variables.name: Rate of CSF secretion by the choroid plexuses

q: Jordan, 16, is hit on the side of the head by a baseball and knocked out briefly. He wakes and seems fine, then an hour later becomes drowsy. A scan shows a lens-shaped clot that stops at the skull's sutures. Which vessel was most likely torn?
options: An artery at the base of the brain
A capillary of the choroid plexus

q: Mr. Kowalski, 81, takes a blood-thinning drug. Three weeks after a minor fall he becomes gradually more confused and complains of headache. A scan shows a thin crescent of blood spread over one hemisphere. Where is the blood?
options: Between the skull and the dura mater
Between the dura mater and the arachnoid mater

q: Ms. Tran, 44, has a sudden, explosive headache she calls the worst of her life, and a stiff neck. Her scan is normal, but a lumbar puncture returns fluid mixed with blood. Where did the bleeding happen?
options: Into the choroid plexus of a lateral ventricle

q: Which meningeal layer is stuck to the surface of the brain and follows it into every sulcus?
options: The inner layer of the dura

q: Which of these would cross the blood–brain barrier most easily?
options: A large protein molecule circulating in the plasma
Sodium ions dissolved in the plasma

q: Which structure is the barrier itself in the blood–brain barrier?
options: The layer of astrocyte end-feet that wraps the outside of each brain capillary
The pia mater covering the brain surface
The capillary endothelial cells sealed by continuous tight junctions
The cells covering the choroid plexus

q: Why is a lumbar puncture needle placed between the third and fourth lumbar vertebrae in an adult?
options: The subarachnoid space is widest in the neck, so the lower back is the only safe alternative
The cord ends at about L1–L2, so below it the space holds only floating nerve roots
The dura mater ends at the third lumbar vertebra, so the needle does not have to pierce it
The choroid plexus in the lower spinal canal makes fresh CSF there

q: Which describe normal CSF compared with blood plasma? Select all that apply.
options: More protein, to keep water in the ventricles

q: In the skull of a healthy person, which space around the brain is a real, fluid-filled space?
options: The space inside the dura's two layers everywhere

q: Hydrocephalus makes an infant's head grow abnormally large, but in an adult it causes headache, vomiting and drowsiness with a normal head size. Why the difference?
options: Adults' arachnoid granulations absorb extra fluid before the ventricles can swell
An infant's skull bones are not yet fused, so the skull expands instead of pressure rising
An infant's ventricles are too small to hold much extra fluid

q: A scan shows that both lateral ventricles and the third ventricle are enlarged, but the fourth ventricle is normal. Where is the blockage most likely to be?
options: At the median and lateral apertures

q: Some toxins in the blood trigger vomiting even though they cannot cross the blood–brain barrier. How?
options: They reach an area on the floor of the fourth ventricle whose capillaries lack the barrier
They dissolve through the tight junctions of brain capillaries
They travel in the cerebrospinal fluid from the lumbar region to the brain
Astrocyte end-feet pick them up and carry them across the capillary wall

q: In this spinal cord cross section, back side at the top, which structure does pointer 7 mark?

On the right, from top to bottom: 1, the shallow midline groove at the back; 2, the white matter between that groove and the dorsal horn; 3, the narrow gray horn reaching toward the back; 4, the small gray bump at the side; 5, the white matter at the side; 6, the tiny hole in the center; 7, the broad gray horn reaching toward the front; 8, the white matter at the front beside the midline; 9, the deep midline groove at the front. q: At about what vertebral level does the spinal cord end in an adult?
options: The first to second lumbar vertebrae

q: What is the cauda equina?
options: The cone-shaped lower end of the spinal cord
The bundle of lumbar and sacral roots hanging in the canal below the cord
The widened part of the cord that supplies the lower limbs
The thin strand of pia that continues below the cord and anchors it to the coccyx

q: Mr. Adeyemi, 41, has a burst disc between his fourth and fifth lumbar vertebrae. His legs are weak, the skin between his thighs is numb, and he cannot pass urine. Which structure is being compressed?
options: The lumbar enlargement of the cord

q: Why is the spinal cord wider in the lower neck than in the middle of the thoracic region?
options: The lower neck segments hold more neurons for the upper limbs
The meninges are thicker in the neck to protect the cord from movement
The central canal widens in the neck to hold more cerebrospinal fluid
The vertebral canal is wider in the neck, so the cord swells to fill it

q: To treat severe pain, a surgeon cuts the dorsal roots of three neighboring segments on the right side. What would you expect in the band of skin and muscles supplied by the middle segment?
options: Paralysis of the muscles, with normal sensation
Loss of sensation, with normal muscle strength
Loss of both sensation and strength
No change, because the ventral roots carry the sensory signals

q: A virus destroys motor neurons in the ventral horns of the lumbar enlargement on both sides. Predict the change in each over the following weeks.

variables.name: Sensation from the skin of the legs

q: Which statements about the dorsal root are true? Select all that apply.
options: It carries sensory axons into the spinal cord
Its ganglion holds the cell bodies of sensory neurons
It carries motor axons out to skeletal muscles
The neurons whose cell bodies sit in its ganglion are pseudounipolar
Its cell bodies lie in the ventral horn

q: Mrs. Jensen, 70, had chickenpox as a child. Now she has a painful, blistering rash in a band around the right side of her chest. Where has the virus been lying dormant?
options: In the ventral horn of the spinal cord
In the lateral horn of the spinal cord

q: A cross section of spinal cord has only a thin rim of white matter around a relatively large area of gray matter, and it has no lateral horns. Which level is it most likely from?
You step on a tack and your leg pulls away. Put the structures the signal passes through in order, from the sole of the foot to the leg muscle.
options: Sensory axon running in from the sole

q: A tract's name begins with "spino-" and ends with the name of a brain region. What does that tell you?
options: It starts in that brain region and carries motor commands down
It stays entirely within the spinal cord, linking one segment to the segments above and below it
It starts in the spinal cord and carries information up to that region
It carries signals out of the cord through the ventral roots

q: This sequence traces a motor command from the brain to a leg muscle. Find the wrong step.
options: The command leaves the motor areas of the cerebral cortex in a descending tract
It runs down the white columns of the spinal cord
It reaches motor neurons in the dorsal horn of a lumbar segment
Their axons leave through the ventral root toward the muscle

q: Fill the gap in the sensory route into the cord: sensory neuron cell body in the dorsal root ganglion → dorsal root → ____ → neurons that relay the signal onward.
Which of these lies outside the central nervous system?
options: The central canal of the spinal cord

q: Why does a newborn's spinal cord end at about the third lumbar vertebra, lower than an adult's?
options: The cord shrinks after birth as unused neurons in its lower segments die
The vertebral column keeps growing longer than the cord after birth
The conus medullaris moves up as the meninges tighten
Newborns have extra lumbar vertebrae that later fuse

q: Name the pinned area.

fig.alt: A side view of the left hemisphere with its functional areas shaded. In the frontal lobe, a green strip just in front of the central sulcus is the primary motor cortex, with a motor association area and a frontal eye field in front of it; a circle low in the frontal lobe marks Broca's area, within the prefrontal cortex. Just behind the central sulcus a dark pink strip is the primary somatosensory cortex, with a sensory association area behind it. A circle in the upper temporal lobe marks Wernicke's area. At the back of the occipital lobe is the primary visual cortex with the visual association area around it, and in the temporal lobe the primary auditory cortex with the auditory association area. A dotted outline where the parietal, temporal and occipital lobes meet marks a general interpretation area.

q: Name the pinned area.

fig.alt: A side view of the left hemisphere with its functional areas shaded. In the frontal lobe, a green strip just in front of the central sulcus is the primary motor cortex, with a motor association area and a frontal eye field in front of it; a circle low in the frontal lobe marks Broca's area, within the prefrontal cortex. Just behind the central sulcus a dark pink strip is the primary somatosensory cortex, with a sensory association area behind it. A circle in the upper temporal lobe marks Wernicke's area. At the back of the occipital lobe is the primary visual cortex with the visual association area around it, and in the temporal lobe the primary auditory cortex with the auditory association area. A dotted outline where the parietal, temporal and occipital lobes meet marks a general interpretation area.

q: Mr. Castillo, 62, understands what is said to him, but his own speech is slow, effortful and made of single words, and he is frustrated by it. His right arm is weak. Where is the damage most likely to be?

Mrs. Lindqvist, 74, speaks quickly and with normal rhythm, but her sentences are full of wrong and made-up words and make little sense. She cannot follow simple spoken instructions and does not seem aware that anything is wrong. Which area is most likely damaged?
A patient speaks fluently and understands speech well, but cannot repeat a short phrase such as "no ifs, ands or buts" after hearing it. Where is the damage most likely to be?
options: In the primary auditory cortex of both hemispheres
In Broca's area, in the lower left frontal lobe, which assembles fluent speech
In the motor areas that control the lips and tongue
In the white matter connecting Wernicke's area to Broca's area

q: Loss of blood flow destroys the hand area of the left primary motor cortex, and nothing else. Predict the change in each.

variables.name: Ability to feel touch on the right hand

q: Late in the evening, after 16 hours awake, you drink a strong coffee. Predict the change in each over the next hour.

variables.name: Binding of adenosine to its receptor proteins in the brain
Time it takes to fall asleep once in bed

q: The lips occupy more of the primary somatosensory cortex than the whole back. What best explains this?
options: The lips are closer to the brain, so their signals arrive stronger
The lips have far more sensory receptors per square centimeter than the back
The back sends most of its touch signals to the cerebellum instead of to the cerebral cortex
The lips are used for speech, so they are mapped in Broca's area as well
misconception: the homunculus is drawn to body size

q: Loss of blood flow damages the medial surface of the right precentral gyrus, inside the longitudinal fissure. Which body part is most likely to be weak?

After damage to his right parietal lobe, Mr. Haddad eats only the food on the right half of his plate and shaves only the right side of his face. His vision and strength test normal. What best explains this?
options: Loss of the primary visual cortex in the right occipital lobe
Damage to Broca's area in the left frontal lobe
Weakness of the left arm from motor cortex damage
Loss of the right hemisphere's attention to the left side of space

q: A woman can describe a face in detail (the shape of the nose, the color of the eyes) but cannot tell that it is her husband's until he speaks. Which statement best explains this?
options: Her primary visual cortex is damaged, so she cannot see the face
Her Wernicke's area is damaged, so she cannot name him
Her hippocampus is damaged, so she has lost all her memories of her husband and their life
Her primary visual cortex works, but part of her visual association area is damaged

q: After encephalitis destroys both of his hippocampi, Mr. Park cannot remember his nurse from one visit to the next. Which ability is he most likely to keep?
options: Remembering what he ate this morning
Learning the names of new staff
Getting better at a new motor skill with daily practice
Recalling a conversation from an hour ago
misconception: memories are stored in the hippocampus

q: A football player is knocked out by a tackle. Afterward he cannot recall the play itself or the few minutes before it, but he remembers the rest of the game and his whole childhood. Which memories did he lose, and why those?
options: The oldest ones, because they are stored in the hippocampus
Procedural memories, because the blow damaged the cerebellum
The most recent ones, because they had not yet been consolidated
Memories scattered at random through his life, because the blow damaged random patches of cortex

q: Which describe REM sleep? Select all that apply.
options: The EEG shows fast, small waves like the awake brain
Most skeletal muscles are paralyzed, but the diaphragm keeps working
Slow, large delta waves dominate the EEG
REM periods are longest in the first cycle of the night

q: According to this graph, when does most N3 (deep) sleep happen?

fig.alt: A graph of sleep stages across an 8-hour night. The vertical axis lists, from top to bottom, awake, REM, N1, N2 and N3 (deep); the horizontal axis shows hours 0 to 8 after lights out. The line drops from awake through N1 and N2 to N3 within the first hour, then cycles up and down about every 90 minutes. Long periods of N3 occur in the first two cycles, a short one in the third, and none after about 4 hours. REM periods, highlighted in color, are short early in the night (about 10 minutes at 1.4 hours) and get longer toward morning (about 40 minutes near 7 hours). Brief awakenings occur late in the night.

q: Using this graph, predict what someone who sleeps only the first four hours of the night misses most.
options: Most of their N3 deep sleep

fig.alt: A graph of sleep stages across an 8-hour night. The vertical axis lists, from top to bottom, awake, REM, N1, N2 and N3 (deep); the horizontal axis shows hours 0 to 8 after lights out. The line drops from awake through N1 and N2 to N3 within the first hour, then cycles up and down about every 90 minutes. Long periods of N3 occur in the first two cycles, a short one in the third, and none after about 4 hours. REM periods, highlighted in color, are short early in the night (about 10 minutes at 1.4 hours) and get longer toward morning (about 40 minutes near 7 hours). Brief awakenings occur late in the night.

q: Why does the EEG show slow, large waves in deep sleep but fast, small waves when you are awake and thinking?
options: In deep sleep, cortical neurons' synaptic potentials rise and fall together
Neurons fire more action potentials in deep sleep than when awake
The skull becomes thinner during sleep, so the signal is less damped
The EEG records muscle activity, which is greatest during sleep

q: Years ago, surgeons cut Ms. Novak's corpus callosum to stop her seizures from spreading. With her eyes closed, she is handed a key in her left hand. What happens?
options: She names it at once and picks it out with either hand
She cannot name it, but her left hand can pick it out
She can neither name it nor pick it out with her left hand
She names it but cannot pick it out with her left hand

q: Put the steps in order for repeating aloud a word you hear, using the classic model of language.
options: The primary auditory cortex receives the sound
White matter carries the word forward to the frontal lobe
Broca's area builds the speech plan
The primary motor cortex drives the muscles of speech

q: This sequence describes how a visual signal becomes recognition of a friend's face. Find the wrong step.
options: Signals from the eyes relay through the thalamus
The primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe receives them first
The primary auditory cortex recognizes the face
Multimodal integration areas link the face with the friend's voice and name

q: After a car crash injures the front of both frontal lobes, Mr. Ruiz, 30, walks, talks and remembers normally, but he is impulsive, makes rude remarks, and cannot stick to a plan. Which area was damaged?
Current research puts the capacity of working memory at about how many chunks of information?
After long-term potentiation, the same amount of glutamate released at a synapse produces a larger EPSP than before. What change in the postsynaptic cell best explains this?
options: Its resting membrane potential has become more negative
Its axon has been freshly myelinated
It has stopped making receptor proteins for glutamate
It has more glutamate receptor proteins in its membrane
